summary: For ages 5–7, children name and recognise iconic Neotropical rainforest animals (jaguars, toucans, sloths, poison dart frogs, howler monkeys, macaws, butterflies) AND place each in its rainforest layer, reusing the four-layer map so naming becomes ecological understanding. Each animal gets one sticky hook (sloth = slowest, howler = loudest, jaguar = big cat of the floor). The central idea: most animal life is in the sunny canopy, and different animals favour different layers because of how they move and where their food is — while a few mobile animals (like butterflies) move between layers.
misconceptions: All rainforest animals live on the ground — most live up in the canopy
Every animal lives everywhere in the forest — different animals favour different layers
Sloths are fast/monkeys — sloths are very slow and are not monkeys
Poison dart frogs are big and dangerous to touch randomly — they are tiny; their bright colour is a warning
Jaguars live in trees all the time — they mainly prowl the forest floor

activities.title: Explore the layered forest alive with animals
steps: Revisit the tall four-layer forest scene (floor, understorey/low damp, canopy, emergent/above) from the layers topic, now populated with iconic animals.

Explore each animal to find out its name, a memorable hook, and which layer it calls home: jaguar padding across the shadowy floor ('big cat, hunts on the ground'); a howler monkey in the canopy ('loudest animal here — lives in the sunny roof'); a sloth ('slowest of all, hangs in the canopy'); a toucan and macaws in the canopy; a tiny bright poison dart frog low in the damp; drifting butterflies that move between layers.
Answer a lift-the-flap style question: 'Which layer has the MOST animals?' and see the crowded canopy highlighted.
activities.insight: The rainforest isn't just full of creatures — most animals have a home layer, and the sunny canopy is the busiest layer of all, while a few mobile animals (like butterflies) move between layers.

activities.title: Sort each animal into its layer
steps: Given a strip or scene with the four layers marked, move each animal card to the layer where it lives (jaguar → floor; howler monkeys/toucans/macaws/sloths → canopy; dart frog → low damp understorey).
Place the butterfly card deliberately as a 'moves-between-layers' animal — it need not sit in a single layer.
Say out loud or recall the one hook for each animal as you place it (sloth = slow, howler = loudest, dart frog = tiny and bright).
activities.insight: Different animals favour different layers; placing them actively checks whether the child has connected each animal to its home rather than just naming it — while a few mobile animals (like butterflies) move between layers.

activities.title: Talk about who lives where — and why
steps: Answer: a howler monkey and a jaguar both live in the rainforest, but not in the same layer — where would you find each one, and why does each live where it does?
Name another animal that lives in the canopy and one that lives on the floor.
Say one special thing about a toucan or a sloth that helps it live where it does.
Discuss: why would a monkey find it hard to live down on the dark forest floor?
activities.insight: Animals mostly live in the layer that suits how they move and where their food is — tree-climbers and leaf- and fruit-eaters up high, ground-hunters down low — so placement has a reason, not just a label.

checkQuestion: A howler monkey and a jaguar both live in the rainforest, but they don't live in the same layer. Where would you find each one, and why does each animal live where it does?
checkAnswer: The howler monkey lives up in the canopy, swinging and feeding among the treetops where there's fruit and light; the jaguar lives down on the forest floor, prowling and hunting on the ground. Animals live in the layer that suits how they move and where their food is — tree-climbers and fruit-eaters up high, ground-hunters down low.
